subject: sociology
topicDisplay: Debates In Contemporary Society Families Relationships Youth Media
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: The pluralist theory of media ownership and content holds that:
options: Owners dictate all media content directly
Media content is shaped largely by consumer demand and a diversity of competing views
The media transmit a single dominant ideology
questions.explain: Pluralists argue that in a competitive market the media give audiences what they want and reflect a plurality of opinions.

questions.q: The hegemonic (dominant-ideology) approach, drawing on Gramsci, differs from instrumental Marxism by arguing that ruling-class dominance in the media is:
options: An unintended outcome of journalists' shared, taken-for-granted middle-class worldview
The result of deliberate owner instruction
questions.explain: Hegemonic/neo-Marxist writers (e.g. the GUMG) see bias as arising not from direct orders but from journalists' largely unconscious consensus assumptions.

questions.q: Cultural pessimists about the new media argue that it:
options: Removed commercial influence from the media
Has democratised access for everyone equally
Reinforces existing inequalities (the digital divide) and concentration of ownership
questions.explain: Pessimists argue new media deepen inequalities through the digital divide and remain dominated by powerful commercial interests.

questions.q: Duncombe and Marsden's concept of the 'triple shift' adds which third element to paid work and housework?
questions.explain: The triple shift adds 'emotion work' — managing the emotional wellbeing of the family — to paid and domestic work.

questions.q: The Glasgow University Media Group is best associated with which approach to the media?
questions.explain: The GUMG's content analysis argued news embodies a dominant ideology through journalists' shared assumptions rather than conspiracy.

questions.q: The concept of 'citizen journalism' associated with new media refers to:
options: Members of the public creating and sharing news content via digital technology
questions.explain: Citizen journalism describes ordinary people using digital tools to gather, report and distribute news, challenging traditional gatekeeping.

questions.q: The 'march of progress' view of childhood argues that:
options: Childhood is increasingly controlled and policed
The position of children has steadily improved over time
questions.explain: The march of progress view holds that children's lives have steadily improved and they are more valued and protected.

questions.q: Charles Murray (New Right) linked the growth of lone-parent families to which alleged problem?
options: A welfare-dependent 'underclass' and boys lacking role models
questions.explain: Murray argued welfare benefits encourage lone parenthood and create a dependent underclass with poor male role models.

questions.q: Marxists are critical of the functionalist view of social policy because they argue policies:
options: Have no effect on family life
Tend to serve the interests of capitalism rather than families equally
questions.explain: Marxists argue social policy ultimately props up capitalism rather than neutrally helping all families.

questions.q: The term 'cultural imperialism' in media globalisation refers to:
options: Equal exchange of culture between all nations
The growth of local media in developing nations
The export of Western, especially American, media and culture overwhelming local cultures
questions.explain: Cultural imperialism describes the dominance of powerful (largely Western) media exporting their values and eroding indigenous cultures.

questions.q: Willmott and Young's thesis that the family is becoming more equal with shared roles is known as the:
questions.explain: Willmott and Young argued the modern family is becoming more 'symmetrical', with conjugal roles more equally shared.

questions.q: The idea that working women perform paid work AND most domestic labour is referred to as the:
questions.explain: The dual burden describes women doing both paid employment and the bulk of unpaid housework.

questions.q: In media studies, the 'digital divide' refers to:
options: The split between print and broadcast media
The gap between fact and opinion online
The division of media ownership between firms
Inequalities in access to and use of new media and the internet
questions.explain: The digital divide describes unequal access to digital technology, often along lines of class, age, region and global inequality.

questions.q: Parsons argued that which family type best 'fits' the needs of modern industrial society?
questions.explain: Parsons claimed the geographically and socially mobile nuclear family fits the needs of industrial society.

questions.q: Which Marxist sociologist argued the family is a haven where workers can be 'themselves' but also reproduces capitalist values like obedience?
questions.explain: Zaretsky argued the family cushions workers but ultimately serves capitalism by reproducing labour and absorbing discontent.

questions.q: Marxist feminists such as Margaret Benston argue that women's unpaid domestic labour primarily benefits whom?
options: Capitalism, by reproducing labour power cheaply
questions.explain: Marxist feminists argue women's unpaid domestic labour reproduces and maintains the labour force at no cost to capitalism.

questions.q: The 'cereal-packet image' of the family refers to:
options: The Marxist view of the family
The idealised conventional nuclear family promoted in adverts and media
questions.explain: Leach's 'cereal-packet family' is the idealised nuclear family image, which most households no longer match.

questions.q: 'Agenda-setting' by the media means that the media:
options: Tell audiences exactly what to think
Always reflect the public's existing priorities
Influence what issues people think about by deciding what to cover
Have no effect on public opinion
questions.explain: Agenda-setting suggests the media shape which topics are seen as important, even if they do not determine opinions on them.

questions.q: Which functionalist sociologist identified four essential functions of the family: sexual, reproductive, economic and educational?
questions.explain: Murdock argued the nuclear family is universal because it performs four essential functions for society.

questions.q: A 'reconstituted' (blended) family is one that:
options: Is headed by a single parent
Is formed when partners with children from previous relationships join together
Consists of a couple with no children
questions.explain: A reconstituted or step-family forms when at least one partner brings a child from a previous relationship.

questions.q: Which of the following is a key reason given for the long-term decline in the birth rate?
options: Falling infant mortality and the changing position of women
questions.explain: Lower infant mortality and changes such as women's education and careers help explain the long-term fall in the birth rate.

questions.q: The 'total fertility rate' (TFR) refers to:
options: The number of deaths per 1,000 per year
The proportion of the population over 65
The number of live births per 1,000 of the population per year
The average number of children women will have during their childbearing years
questions.explain: The TFR is the average number of children a woman will have over her fertile years; the UK's has fallen long-term.

questions.q: A 'moral panic', as theorised by Stanley Cohen, involves:
options: A purely economic crisis in the media industry
Exaggerated media reaction to a group, amplifying deviance and prompting calls for control
A gradual, balanced media discussion of an issue
questions.explain: Cohen's study of mods and rockers showed how media exaggeration creates disproportionate public concern and can amplify the very deviance it condemns.

questions.q: The 'hypodermic syringe' model of media effects assumes that:
options: The media inject messages directly into a passive audience, producing immediate effects
Audiences use media to satisfy their own needs
Effects are filtered through opinion leaders
Audiences actively interpret media in varied ways
questions.explain: The hypodermic model treats audiences as passive and assumes media messages have a direct, uniform and powerful effect.

questions.q: Stuart Hall et al.'s 'Policing the Crisis' analysed the moral panic over 'mugging' as serving to:
options: Divert attention from the crisis of capitalism by scapegoating young black men
Reflect genuine consumer demand for crime news
questions.explain: Hall argued the mugging panic functioned ideologically to legitimate increased control during a crisis and shifted blame onto a racialised folk devil.

questions.q: Postman and others argue childhood is now disappearing or changing, partly due to:
options: The decline of the nuclear family
Children's growing access to the adult world via media
questions.explain: Postman argued the boundary between childhood and adulthood is blurring, partly through media access ('the disappearance of childhood').

questions.q: The rise in cohabitation is best interpreted as evidence of which broad trend?
options: The growing diversity of family and household forms
The return of the extended family
questions.explain: Increasing cohabitation reflects greater diversity and changing attitudes towards marriage.

questions.q: Which feminist perspective sees the family as the main site of women's oppression and patriarchy, sometimes advocating separatism?
questions.explain: Radical feminists argue the family and marriage are key institutions of patriarchal oppression.

questions.q: 'News values' are best defined as:
options: The profit margins of news organisations
The political opinions of media owners
The criteria journalists use to judge whether an event is newsworthy
questions.explain: News values (e.g. immediacy, negativity, personalisation, elite persons) are the implicit criteria by which events are selected and prioritised as news.

questions.q: In Stanley Cohen's work, a 'folk devil' is:
options: A group defined as a threat to societal values, becoming a focus of public concern
A media owner who manipulates the news
An opinion leader in the two-step flow
questions.explain: Cohen described folk devils as the deviant groups (e.g. mods and rockers) demonised by the media during a moral panic.
